title: Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare Proposes Amendments to Medical Devices Rules, 2017 to Promote Ease of Doing Business
subtitle: Proposed amendments seek to simplify regulatory requirements, standardize testing fees and facilitate faster market access for eligible medical devices
body_text:
The Government has undertaken key regulatory reforms in the medical device sector to promote Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) by simplifying regulatory requirements, enhancing transparency and facilitating timely access to advanced and innovative medical technologies in the country.
The reforms include amendments to the Medical Devices Rules, 2017 in three key areas—simplification of provisions relating to outsourced sterilization of medical devices, introduction of uniform testing fees and inclusion of the European Union among recognized jurisdictions for waiver of clinical investigation requirements.
Under the amended provisions of Rule 44 of the Medical Devices Rules, 2017, manufacturers availing outsourced sterilization facilities will no longer be required to obtain a separate loan licence under Rule 25, provided that the sterilization facility holds a valid licence under the Medical Devices Rules, 2017.
Earlier, manufacturers without an in-house sterilization facility were required to obtain a separate loan licence for sterilization activities. The amended provision is expected to reduce regulatory compliance requirements, documentation, approval timelines and associated costs, while enabling manufacturers to efficiently avail specialized sterilization facilities.
Further, a Ninth Schedule has been inserted in the Medical Devices Rules, 2017 prescribing uniform fees for the testing of medical devices by Medical Device Testing Laboratories. The measure will establish a standardized and transparent fee structure across laboratories, reducing ambiguity and variations in testing charges.
The standardized fee structure is expected to provide greater predictability to manufacturers and importers, minimize disputes, ensure equitable treatment of stakeholders and further strengthen transparency and efficiency in the medical device regulatory framework.
In another significant reform, Rule 63 of the Medical Devices Rules, 2017 has been amended to include the European Union (EU) among the recognized stringent regulatory jurisdictions for waiver of clinical investigation requirements for medical devices without predicate devices.
The provision presently recognizes the United States of America, United Kingdom, Australia, Canada and Japan. The inclusion of the European Union will facilitate faster access in India to eligible medical devices that have already been approved in the EU, while reducing regulatory burden and timelines for importers and manufacturers.
The reforms are expected to simplify regulatory processes, reduce compliance costs, enhance transparency and predictability, and facilitate the timely availability of advanced and innovative medical devices in the country.
The measures mark an important step towards strengthening the medical device regulatory ecosystem and promoting greater international regulatory convergence, while continuing to ensure the highest standards of quality, safety and performance of medical devices.
The Official Gazette notification may be accessed through this link: https://egazette.gov.in/WriteReadData/2026/275637.pdf

ministry.name: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare

enrichment.summary: The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has proposed amendments to the Medical Devices Rules, 2017 to promote Ease of Doing Business by simplifying regulations in three areas: manufacturers using outsourced sterilization facilities no longer need a separate loan licence under Rule 25 if the sterilization facility itself is licensed; a new Ninth Schedule prescribes uniform testing fees across Medical Device Testing Laboratories; and the European Union has been added under Rule 63 to the list of recognized stringent regulatory jurisdictions (alongside the USA, UK, Australia, Canada and Japan) for waiver of clinical investigation requirements for devices without predicate devices. These changes aim to reduce compliance costs, timelines and ambiguity while enabling faster market access for medical devices already approved in the EU.
enrichment.context:
The Medical Devices Rules, 2017, notified under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, govern the regulatory framework for manufacture, import, sale and clinical investigation of medical devices in India, and are administered by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO). India's medical device sector has historically faced criticism for regulatory duplication, inconsistent testing fees across laboratories, and long approval timelines, which raised compliance costs for manufacturers and importers, particularly for innovative or globally-approved devices seeking entry into the Indian market. The government has been progressively expanding the list of 'stringent regulatory authorities' whose approvals can substitute for local clinical trials, a practice aligned with global regulatory convergence and reliance principles promoted by bodies like the International Medical Device Regulators Forum (IMDRF).

This reform fits within the broader Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) agenda that has driven changes across sectors, including deregulation, decriminalization of minor offences, and single-window clearances. For the health sector specifically, faster access to devices already vetted by EU regulators (known for rigorous standards under the EU Medical Device Regulation) is expected to benefit patients by expediting availability of advanced diagnostic and therapeutic technologies, while easing the compliance burden on domestic manufacturers who rely on third-party sterilization services rather than costly in-house facilities.
syllabus_topics: GS Paper 2 - Government Policies and Interventions

prelims_questions.question:
With reference to the Medical Devices Rules, 2017, consider the following countries/regions recognized as stringent regulatory jurisdictions for waiver of clinical investigation requirements after recent amendments:
1. United States of America
2. European Union
3. China
4. Japan
Which of the above are correctly recognized under Rule 63?
prelims_questions.explanation: The recognized stringent regulatory jurisdictions under amended Rule 63 are USA, UK, Australia, Canada, Japan, and now the EU; China is not included.

prelims_questions.question: The 'Ninth Schedule' recently inserted into the Medical Devices Rules, 2017 pertains to which of the following?
options: Classification of medical devices by risk category
Uniform fees for testing of medical devices by Medical Device Testing Laboratories
Guidelines for clinical investigation of new devices
prelims_questions.explanation: The Ninth Schedule prescribes a standardized, uniform fee structure for testing of medical devices across Medical Device Testing Laboratories.

mains_questions.question: Discuss how regulatory reforms in the medical devices sector, such as recognition of stringent regulatory jurisdictions and standardized testing fees, contribute to the Ease of Doing Business in India's healthcare manufacturing ecosystem.

Examine the significance of regulatory convergence with international standards (such as EU medical device approvals) for ensuring both patient safety and timely market access in India's medical device sector.
mains_questions.gs_paper: GS Paper 2 - Government Policies and Interventions

study_notes.reason: The release carries a testable factual core (specific rule numbers, the list of stringent regulatory jurisdictions, the new Ninth Schedule) alongside a clear analytical thread on India's Ease of Doing Business and regulatory convergence strategy in the health sector.

prelims.point: Medical Devices Rules, 2017 are notified under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and administered by CDSCO
prelims.why_important: Tests the legal basis and regulatory authority for medical device governance in India, a common UPSC pattern of linking rules to parent acts.

prelims.point: Rule 63 recognized stringent regulatory jurisdictions for waiver of clinical investigation now include USA, UK, Australia, Canada, Japan and (newly) the European Union
prelims.why_important: UPSC frequently frames statement-based questions on lists of recognized bodies/jurisdictions; the EU's recent addition is the key new fact from this release.

prelims.point: A new Ninth Schedule has been inserted in the Medical Devices Rules, 2017 prescribing uniform testing fees across Medical Device Testing Laboratories
prelims.why_important: Specific schedule insertions are occasionally tested to check whether candidates track amendments to named rules.

prelims.point: Amended Rule 44 removes the need for a separate loan licence under Rule 25 for manufacturers using outsourced, already-licensed sterilization facilities
prelims.why_important: Tests understanding of licensing simplification mechanisms distinguishing 'loan licence' requirements from facility-level licensing.

mains.point: Reliance on stringent regulatory authorities (like EU, US, UK) for clinical waiver reflects India's move toward global regulatory convergence rather than duplicative domestic testing
mains.theme: Regulatory convergence and Ease of Doing Business
mains.analytical_use: Useful for questions on how India is aligning its regulatory framework with international standards (e.g., IMDRF reliance principles) to balance safety with market access.

mains.point: Simplification of sterilization licensing reduces compliance costs, documentation and approval timelines for manufacturers without in-house facilities
mains.theme: Ease of doing business in manufacturing
mains.analytical_use: Can be used in answers on deregulation and reducing compliance burden as part of India's EoDB reforms across sectors.

mains.point: Uniform testing fee structure aims to reduce ambiguity, disputes and unequal treatment among manufacturers across different testing laboratories
mains.analytical_use: Supports discussion on governance reforms that improve predictability and reduce discretion/disputes in regulatory administration.

mains.point: Faster market access to EU-approved devices could benefit patients through quicker availability of advanced diagnostic/therapeutic technologies, but raises questions about domestic testing capacity being bypassed
mains.analytical_use: Can be used to critically examine trade-offs between faster access to technology and maintaining independent domestic safety verification standards.
